prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language oeuvre of densely patterned prose that builds vast inner cosmologies out of memory, the body and dream, with roots in poetry.

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu alone. My citation wording changes slightly, as explained below. The case rests on the whole authorship, not on a single title. From public knowledge of Blinding (the Orbitor sequence) and Solenoid, I understand the voice to be unmistakable, with formal ambition carried across very large structures in which memory, the body and metaphysical speculation form one imaginative architecture. The late major novels suggest a consolidated oeuvre, so I do not see a timing problem. A single-name citation is unambiguous and needs no national or political symbolism. The six-of-six alignment in round 1 is not merit, and I do not count it as such. I tested my position against the strongest alternatives the exchange offered: Adonis and Tawada on linguistic transformation, Carson on formal reinvention, Can Xue on radical consistency, and Michon on sentence-level concentration. Each of these has a serious literary case, and each is limited, for me, by an evidentiary gap rather than by a demonstrated weakness. Those gaps are access to the original language, the scope of a citation, or the cumulative weight of a compact or fragmentary body of work. I have no comparable evidence that would reverse the Cărtărescu judgment. On the chair's question about citation scope, I now favor anchoring the citation on the prose, with poetry named only as a root. I adopt that wording because the claim of one imaginative project across genres is partly inferred, and the poetry is thinner in translation. I do not think the committee can currently weigh the poetry as an independent pillar.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that the achievement lives in dense, rhythmic Romanian prose that I can judge only through translation. I cannot confirm that the patterning and musicality match the critical consensus. The maximalist long forms may amount to accumulation rather than depth. I have no volume-by-volume evidence showing that the later novels deepen the earlier image systems rather than recirculate them. That is the chair's first question, and I cannot settle it from public knowledge. If the committee weighed formal reinvention of a language or genre above expansion of an established visionary mode, Adonis or Tawada would have a stronger claim than I currently give them. My own preference for Cărtărescu partly reflects that I can judge his development more confidently than theirs, which is a limit of my access and not a ruling on their work.

responses.point: Carlberg argues that the Cărtărescu citation should be anchored on the novels, with the poetry as the origin of the vision and not an independently assessed pillar. She also says she would want colleagues who read Japanese or German to say which works carry the Tawada case.
responses.response: I accept the first point, and it is the main reason my citation wording changes. In round 1 I wrote that the prose was 'rooted in poetry', but I cannot verify that from the translated poetry. The citation should therefore say what the committee can assess, the prose, and name poetry only as a root. On Tawada, your request is fair and I cannot meet it fully. I rank her high because the bilingual practice looks to me like a formal principle, and my evidence is the representative works named in the entry, The Emissary and Memoirs of a Polar Bear. That is not a whole-oeuvre judgment in two languages. I therefore hold her as an alternative and not as a preference, and I treat your hesitation as a legitimate check on my second-place opening rank.

responses.point: Palm proposes a concrete test for Cărtărescu: do the long novels develop their image systems or only recirculate them? She says she sees a visible arc from the poetry through the Blinding sequence to Solenoid, and that she cannot judge whether Can Xue has a comparable arc because of partial translation.
responses.response: I adopt your test as the right one, and I raised the repetition risk myself in round 1. From public knowledge, I understand Solenoid to be treated as a late culmination and not as a restatement, but that is reputation and not a reading I can document. I therefore hold the Cărtărescu judgment as the best-supported option on the list and not as a settled one. Your point about Can Xue also affects my own ranking. I put her fifth because I cannot tell whether four decades of method show deepening. Since you apply the same test to both writers and find the arc visible in one and unjudgeable in the other, I think the asymmetry is an evidentiary one, and I would not use it to dismiss her.

responses.point: Mattson calls the claim that poetry is the base of Cărtărescu's prose project a hypothesis, not an established fact. She also says a Cărtărescu citation should rest on the prose and not on a role as a representative of Romanian or European letters, and that political commentary must be separated from literary assessment for every candidate.
responses.response: I agree on all three points and have changed my wording accordingly. Treating the poetry link as a hypothesis is more honest than my round-1 phrasing, which presented it as settled. I also agree that the standard applies across the list. I would extend it to my own reasoning: I should not let the symbolic weight of a Romanian laureate, or of any other language or region, stand in for literary argument. The same applies to Adonis. His public positions belong outside the literary case, and the case has to rest on the poems and his poetics, which I can judge only unevenly through translation.

responses.point: Olsson says durability across the longest works cannot be settled from public reputation alone. He also says a Carson citation would need a defined body of original literary work, and that he would take her more seriously if the scope could be drawn around her original poetry.
responses.response: I agree that reputation cannot settle durability, and I accept it as an unresolved reservation. Where I differ slightly is on weight. The uncertainty applies to every candidate whose achievement lies in large forms, and Cărtărescu is the one for whom I can at least name the works. On Carson, your scope question is the decisive one for me too. I rank her fourth because the original poetry, verse narrative and essays would have to carry a lifetime citation without scholarship, translation or book-design. Autobiography of Red and Nox show real formal invention. I still cannot see how many short or fragmentary books would add up to the cumulative weight that the Cărtărescu sequence shows.

uncertainties: Whether the density, rhythm and musicality of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survive translation, and whether the long novels deepen their image systems or recirculate them. I cannot settle this from public knowledge.
How much of his poetry and early work is available in translation. This limits how much weight the poetry can bear in the citation, and it is why I now name it only as a root.
Whether Tawada's bilingual oeuvre can be fairly judged without full competence in both Japanese and German. I also do not know how representative the translated works are.
How much of Adonis's formal achievement in Arabic prosody can be judged by non-Arabic readers, and whether his reputation reflects influence or the poems themselves.

Whether Can Xue's consistent method reflects rigor or repetition across a large, partly translated output, and whether Carson's hybrid or short works and Michon's compact oeuvre carry enough cumulative weight under 'significance across the writer's body of work'.

The chair asked whether P000 would be preferable. On the evidence in this exchange I do not think so. The reservations about Cărtărescu concern translation and the limits of my access, not the writer's significance. I hold that view with the caveat that no member has read the corpus for this exercise.

I have not independently verified any bibliography or source, and I rely on public knowledge and colleagues' stated views. A co-opted member's voting status, which affects the modeling of this vote, is undocumented.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any shortlisted writer is documented in my supplied profile. The documented ties are collegial: I was elected in the 2019 renewal round with Ellen Mattson, and I serve on the committee with Olsson, Mattson, Sem-Sandberg and Palm. Institutional engagements with Swedish Institute, Arts Council and Nordic Council of Ministers programmes do not involve any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist is context, not evidence of a preference. I disclose, without adjudicating it, that I have publicly said the Academy has overlooked many significant women's authorships. I do not use gender, nationality or language as a criterion of merit in this configuration, and my choice rests on the literary criteria above.
